candidates.title: Loopjacking: Hijacking Human-in-the-Loop Approval
candidates.venue: arXiv preprint (cs.CR primary, cs.MA cross-list); not yet peer-reviewed
candidates.citationVelocity: submitted 2026-09-17, announced in Monday 2026-09-21 batch; no citation data available
communitySignals: no HF Daily Papers / Papers with Code listing found
credibilityEvidence: Section 1 gives a falsifiable definition (qualifying-trace criteria) distinguishing Loopjacking from ordinary persuasion/prompt injection
reproduces post-approval state-substitution in 7 Agno AgentOS releases and 12 LangGraph Agent Server versions, and representation mismatch in OpenClaw 2026.2.23 (fixed in 2026.2.24)
includes OpenAI Agents SDK 0.22.0/0.22.2 as a negative control that resists the attack
explicit scope disclaimer: 'These results do not estimate ecosystem prevalence'
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: concrete, reproducible findings on named product versions with a public evidence archive, but the population is a purposive sample chosen to test mechanically different approval paths, not a survey of the agent-framework ecosystem
reproducibilityEvidence: GitHub evidence archive with exact tested versions and configs (github.com/adithyan-ak/loopjacking)
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: the narrow claim (these specific products/versions exhibit this exact failure class) is fully supported by the reproduced evidence and the negative control
candidates.primaryLimitation: comparative, not representative sample; author explicitly disclaims any ecosystem-wide prevalence estimate
candidates.presentationReason: attack taxonomy, attacker model, and defenses are precisely defined with a testable qualifying-trace criterion
candidates.reason: Concrete, reproduced security failure in real, named agent-framework releases (Agno, LangGraph, OpenClaw) with a negative control and public evidence archive; forms the vulnerability-discovery angle of today's authorization-boundary theme.

candidates.title: APort Vault: Benchmarking AI Agent Payment Authorization with the Open Agent Passport
candidates.venue: arXiv preprint (cs.CR primary, cs.AI secondary); not yet peer-reviewed
communitySignals: full 225,964-row dataset + scoring code + pre-registration released at huggingface.co/datasets/aporthq/vault-benchmark-v1 (CC BY 4.0)
credibilityEvidence: 4,371 human-authored attacks from a live public CTF against a real payment agent, replayed across 14 models from 8 labs, 5 policy levels, 2 replay tracks = 225,964 completed evaluations

deterministic outcome metric (executed tool calls), not a judge score; a 2-judge audit panel is reported separately with its own reliability numbers (pooled kappa 0.772, one judge missing 35.6% of confirmed outcomes) precisely to show why the deterministic metric is used

session-clustered bootstrap CIs, pre-registration with disclosed addenda, explicit 'what this paper does not claim' section (scoped to payments/one tool schema/simulated bank; not evidence about exfiltration, code execution or inter-agent delegation)
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: large N, real adversarial corpus (not researcher-authored), matched-triple statistical comparison, and an audited outcome metric; still a single simulated-bank deployment, not a cross-deployment field study
reproducibilityEvidence: 225,964 evaluation rows, level passports, scoring code, analysis script and pre-registration publicly released on HuggingFace Datasets under CC BY 4.0
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: the headline claim (a deterministic pre-action authorization layer, not model choice, is what stops unpermitted transfers) is directly read off executed tool calls, not inferred
candidates.primaryLimitation: scoped to one tool schema (payments) in one simulated bank; authors explicitly note the zero-unpermitted-transfer result assumes a correctly configured policy engine, not that authorization layers cannot be misconfigured
candidates.presentationReason: five-stage outcome accounting, explicit scope section, and a dedicated section on what the paper does not claim make the claim boundary unusually legible
candidates.reason: Largest and most rigorous empirical piece of the cluster: shows at benchmark scale that tool-boundary enforcement, not model selection, is what actually blocks unauthorized agent payments, and released full artifacts for independent replication.

candidates.title: Authorization Revocation for Long-Running AI Agents: Root-Scoped Quiescence under Delegation and Asynchronous Execution
candidates.venue: arXiv preprint (cs.PL primary, cs.AI + cs.CR secondary); not yet peer-reviewed
candidates.institution: Accentrust (Vancouver) + Georgia Institute of Technology + University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
communitySignals: no HF Daily Papers / Papers with Code listing found
credibilityEvidence: formal definitions and six proved properties (post-cut issuer non-expansion, support-sound projection, compositional soundness, independent-support preservation, merge-order independence, crash/replay stability) under stated assumptions
explicit Section 1.4 scope statement excluding global idleness, rollback, and business-level task completion from the certified guarantee
self-implemented late-effect test suite matches 17/17 registered outcomes, and a separately implemented checker verifies the same 17 traces and rejects 44/44 mutated regressions
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: the formal proofs are complete under the paper's own model, but empirical validation is a small (17-trace), self-authored test suite rather than a deployment on existing agent-framework cancellation paths (MCP/A2A/OAuth), which the paper explicitly distinguishes itself from
reproducibilityEvidence: test-suite outcomes and checker results are reported in-paper with exact counts; no public code repository link found in the abstract/intro sections read
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: the formal safety properties are well-scoped and explicitly bounded, but the practical claim (this closes the gap left by MCP/A2A cancellation and OAuth revocation in production) rests on a narrow self-authored test suite, not a demonstrated integration
candidates.primaryLimitation: small, self-implemented test suite (17 traces); no evidence yet of integration with a real multi-provider agent runtime
candidates.presentationReason: the formal apparatus (root-epoch atoms, antichains of minimal sufficient root sets, cutset certificates) is precisely defined but demands background in distributed-systems formalism; the worked counterexample in Section 1.1 is the clearest entry point
candidates.reason: Only candidate in the pool that formally defines what 'an agent's authorization is actually revoked' means once credentials, delegated tasks, and provider-side operations can outlive the initiating process; supplies the conceptual vocabulary the other two empirical/attack papers in this cluster lack. Selected with lowered claim strength (conditional pass, preliminary evidence maturity) reflecting its narrow self-authored validation.
